title: The History of Orthodontics
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of orthodontics, from ancient observations of crooked teeth (Hippocrates, Egyptian mummies with gold bands, Celsus, Pliny) through Pierre Fauchard's early-1700s braces and pelican forceps, the 19th-century shift to scientific practice with headgear, expanders, and the wire crib, Edward Angle's school and classification system, Raymond Begg's stainless steel work, and modern braces, self-ligating braces, and invisible aligners. They also discuss the cosmetic versus medical debate, orthodontic statistics and costs, and the difficulty of studying benefits. The episode closes with a listener mail about medical terminology and a live show request from Gabe in Ann Arbor.

segments.title: Opening banter and why teeth are crooked
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the orthodontics topic, joke about teeth and Hollywood's perfect-teeth standard, and explain that crooked teeth stem from having the same number of teeth in a smaller jaw after humans evolved larger brains and softer diets.

segments.title: Ancient orthodontic observations
segments.summary: Hippocrates wrote about crowded teeth causing problems, and Egyptian mummies appear to have gold bands tied with catgut to move teeth.

segments.title: Roman-era tooth practices
segments.summary: Celsus advised plucking baby teeth and pressing adult teeth into place; Pliny suggested filing teeth to fix alignment, a practice still used for bite adjustment.

segments.title: Pierre Fauchard and early braces
segments.summary: Pierre Fauchard in the early 1700s filed teeth for space (inner proximal stripping), applied steady pressure, and used waxed silk or wire to tie crooked teeth to neighbors, the basis of modern braces. Bite equilibration is also discussed.

segments.title: Pelican forceps, early dental care, and attitudes toward showing teeth
segments.summary: Fauchard adapted the pelican forceps for moving teeth and once fractured a young woman's tooth. He recommended a wine and honey mouthwash. Hosts explain that showing teeth in 18th-century portraits was considered impolite.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the next section.

segments.title: 19th-century orthodontics: naming, schools, headgear, wire crib
segments.summary: Le Foulon coined the term orthodontics. Dentists practiced it as part of general dentistry until Edward Angle's school in the early 1900s. Headgear used the skull as an anchor, and the chin cup pulled the lower jaw back. Christophe François de la Barre created the wire crib.

segments.title: Palatal expanders and Norman Kingsley
segments.summary: Norman Kingsley of New York City was an influential early orthodontist interested in facial symmetry and wrote a treatise on oral deformities in 1880. Expanders widened narrow jaws by slowly cranking an appliance on the palate; hosts relate it to a daughter's treatment.

segments.title: Edward Angle, research, and the orthodontic rift
segments.summary: John Nutting Farrar experimented on animals to find safe expansion limits. Edward Angle created the Angle system of prefab appliances in 1887, the occlusal classification system, the Society of Orthodontists, and the first orthodontic journal. A debate arose over early versus adult treatment.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Break before resuming the modern braces discussion.

segments.title: Modern braces, Raymond Begg, and stainless steel
segments.summary: Raymond Begg, an Angle student practicing in Adelaide in the 1930s, popularized stainless steel wire over precious metals. Stainless steel arrived in the US around 1956. Hosts discuss the rise in braces use and the evolution from banded to ceramic and colored braces.

segments.title: Self-ligating braces, invisible aligners, and fashion braces
segments.summary: Self-ligating braces use snap-in brackets instead of elastic ties. Invisible aligners were invented by Zia Chishti and Kelsey Wright around 1997 and launched as Invisalign within three years. Online-ordered aligners drew criticism from the orthodontic community. Fashion braces and gap bands are mentioned.

segments.title: Orthodontic statistics, costs, and the medical-versus-cosmetic debate
segments.summary: Hosts discuss 2022 figures showing about 3.15 million children aged 8 to 17 in treatment, and US spending of roughly ten billion dollars. They speculate that health claims may help insurance coverage, and note the difficulty of randomized trials on benefits and selection bias.

segments.title: Listener mail: medical terminology and Ann Arbor live show
segments.summary: Gabe, a recent medical school graduate, writes about the term 'purulent' in place of a crude word, and asks for a live show in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Hosts respond and sign off.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close with the show credit and listener email address.
